lesson_title: Halfway Up Two Rafters: the Midpoint Theorem
hook_text: A builder cuts the brace on the ground, before he climbs. He already knows the length. Here's how.
clip_script: A roof going up. Two rafters leaning together at the top, and one long beam across the bottom — six metres of it. The builder needs a brace nailed straight across from one rafter to the other. So he marks the halfway point on the left rafter, marks the halfway point on the right rafter, and nails a piece between them. Two things happen every single time. One: the brace comes out dead level with the beam below it. Not roughly — exactly parallel. Two: the brace is three metres. Half the beam. He could have cut it on the ground before he ever climbed the ladder. That's the whole theorem: mark the middle of two sides of a triangle, join those marks, and the piece you drew is parallel to the third side and half its length. Beam ten metres, brace five. Beam seven, brace three and a half. And why half? Cut along the brace, take the little top triangle, spin it a half-turn about the mark on the rafter — it slots in beside the bottom piece and makes a parallelogram. Two brace-lengths along the top, one beam along the bottom, and a parallelogram's top equals its bottom. Two braces equal one beam. That's your half, and it was never a guess.
visual_style: A township house frame at golden hour: rafters rising, chalk marks appearing at the halfway points, a brace snapping into place, then the top triangle rotating down to complete a glowing parallelogram.
pacing: Unhurried through the marking, a sharp beat on 'three metres', slow and deliberate on the spin.
